title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Projects, Stacks and State
Every Pulumi command you run answers three questions before it touches a cloud API: which program (the project), which copy of it (the stack), and where is the record of what already exists (the backend and its state). Get those three straight and the rest of Pulumi is “write a program that declares resources”. Get them wrong and you deploy staging’s code into production’s state.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Learning goals

Read a Pulumi.yaml and say which runtime and entrypoint it selects
Create, select, rename and remove stacks, and explain fully qualified stack names
Export stack outputs and consume them from another project with a StackReference
Choose between Pulumi Cloud and a DIY backend, and know what pulumi refresh does and does not do




Two projects, three stacks each, linked by stack references; every stack has its own state in the backend.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
section: Projects: the program and its Pulumi.yaml
text:
Projects: the program and its Pulumi.yaml
A project is any directory containing a Pulumi.yaml. At run time Pulumi walks up from the current directory to the nearest one, and that file decides the project. pulumi new creates it.
name: webserver
runtime: python
description: A minimal Pulumi program.

name is the project name. It also namespaces configuration keys (next chapter).
runtime is one of nodejs, python, go, dotnet, java, yaml or hcl.
Each runtime finds its entrypoint by its own convention: __main__.py (or setup.py) for Python, package.json for Node, the build tool for Go, .NET and Java, .tf files for HCL.

The file name must start with a capital P. Either .yaml or .yml works.
For compiled languages you can skip the build at deploy time by pointing at a prebuilt binary:
name: my-project
runtime:
  name: go
  options:
    binary: mybinary
Paths. File paths inside a program are relative to the working directory. If the program must find files next to Pulumi.yaml regardless of where it was launched, use pulumi.get_root_directory() and convert the result to a path relative to the working directory, so plans don’t differ between machines.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
section: Stacks: many instances of one program
text:
Stacks: many instances of one program
A stack is an isolated, independently configured instance of the project’s program, typically dev, staging, production, or one per feature branch. Each stack has its own configuration and its own state. The program is shared.
pulumi stack init staging     # create and select
pulumi stack ls               # list stacks of the nearest project
pulumi stack select dev       # change the active stack
pulumi stack                  # show the active stack's resources and outputs
The commands config, preview, up and destroy act on the active stack. Pass --stack (or -s) in scripts and pipelines rather than relying on whatever was selected last.

Names
Stack names may contain letters, digits, hyphens, underscores and periods, and must be unique within a project. A stack can be written three ways:



Form
Meaning




dev
Current user or default organization, nearest project


acme/dev
Organization acme, nearest project


acme/webserver/dev
Fully qualified: organization, project, stack



On a DIY backend the organization part is always the literal organization. Backends initialised by a CLI older than v3.61.0 only understand the short form until upgraded with pulumi state upgrade.


Renaming has consequences
pulumi stack rename production changes the value of pulumi.get_stack(). If your program uses the stack name in resource names, the next pulumi up proposes replacements. Read the preview. Sometimes creating a new stack is the safer operation.
A rename across projects (acme/old-project/prod to acme/new-project/prod) needs two manual follow-ups: change name in Pulumi.yaml, and rename project-namespaced keys in Pulumi.<stack>.yaml (for example old-project:database to new-project:database). Skip the second step and the program silently sees those values as unset.


Removing
pulumi destroy deletes the stack’s resources. pulumi stack rm then deletes the empty stack, its history and its Pulumi.<stack>.yaml. pulumi stack rm --force removes a stack that still has resources, orphaning them. Do not.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Outputs: what a stack publishes
A stack exports values from the top level of the program:
import pulumi

pulumi.export("x", "hello")
pulumi.export("o", {"num": 42})
From the documentation (not run here), reading them back looks like:
$ pulumi stack output x
hello
$ pulumi stack output --json
{
  "x": "hello",
  "o": {
      "num": 42
  }
}
Outputs are effectively JSON-serialised and resolved after the update finishes. Export IDs and names, not whole resource objects, which serialise to large blobs. Secret outputs display as [secret] unless you pass --show-secrets.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Stack references: wiring projects together
Large systems split into projects by lifecycle and ownership, for example infra (network, cluster) and services (apps deployed onto it). The pairing is by environment: acme/infra/production feeds acme/services/production. A StackReference reads another stack’s outputs:
import pulumi
from pulumi import StackReference

env = pulumi.get_stack()
infra = StackReference(f"acme/infra/{env}")

kubeconfig = infra.require_output("kubeConfig")
Use the fully qualified name. Pulumi records the dependency between stacks. Choose the reader carefully:








Method
Behaviour
Use




require_output
Fails the deployment if the output is missing
Default choice; turns a typo into an error


get_output
Returns an output wrapping None if missing
Only when absence is expected and handled


get_output_details
Awaitable; returns .value or .secret_value directly
When program logic needs the raw value. Python needs an async entrypoint and SDK 3.254.0 or later



The referenced stack’s outputs are its public interface. Renaming an output is a breaking change for every consumer, just like renaming a function.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
State and backends
Each stack’s state is Pulumi’s record of the resources it manages. preview and up diff the program against that record, not against the live cloud. The state lives in a backend:

Pulumi Cloud (the default, also self-hostable): pulumi login with no argument. Updates go through a transactional API with full history.
DIY: object storage you run (S3 or compatible such as MinIO or Ceph, Azure Blob, GCS), a PostgreSQL database, or the local filesystem. pulumi login <backend-url>, for example pulumi login file://~ for local files.

Avoid typing the URL every time by setting PULUMI_BACKEND_URL or a backend.url in Pulumi.yaml. pulumi whoami -v shows the user and the backend in use. Credentials for backends are stored in ~/.pulumi/credentials.json. Your cloud credentials are never stored in state. They stay where the CLI runs.
With a DIY backend you take on access control, encryption at rest, backups and auditing yourself. Checkpoint history lives under .pulumi/history/, but blob storage is not transactional, so some partial failures cannot be recovered automatically the way Pulumi Cloud recovers them.
Moving a stack between backends is pulumi stack migrate (CLI v3.254.0 or later). Log in to the target and name the source:
pulumi login                          # target: Pulumi Cloud
pulumi stack migrate file://~ my-app-production
It copies the latest checkpoint and configuration, re-encrypts secrets with the target’s secrets provider, and leaves the source untouched.

Drift and refresh
Pulumi does not query every resource on every run. That is a deliberate choice for speed, predictability and explicit control. A console edit is invisible until you run:
pulumi refresh              # update state from the cloud; changes no infrastructure
pulumi preview --refresh    # refresh, then show what up would do
pulumi up --refresh         # refresh, then converge to the program
After a refresh, the next up reverts out-of-band changes unless you also change the program to keep them.


Raw state
pulumi stack export --file stack.json and pulumi stack import --file stack.json give you the JSON checkpoint for inspection or emergency repair. An incorrect import can orphan resources. Export first, keep the copy, and prefer the pulumi state subcommands for targeted edits.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Diagnosis








Symptom
Likely cause
Check




up acts on the wrong environment
Active stack was not the one you assumed
pulumi stack ls (the * marks the active one); pass --stack


CLI says no project (Pulumi.yaml) was found
Running outside the project tree
ls Pulumi.yaml in the directory or a parent


Preview proposes replacing everything after a rename
Stack name used in resource names
Revert the rename, or accept replacement deliberately


Config values silently missing after rename
Project-namespaced keys still carry the old name
Inspect Pulumi.<stack>.yaml


StackReference fails
Wrong qualified name, missing permission, or output not exported
pulumi stack output -s org/project/stack


Stacks “disappeared”
Logged in to a different backend
pulumi whoami -v


Plan ignores a console change
No refresh
pulumi preview --refresh

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Operational care

One project per lifecycle and owner. One stack per environment. Do not encode environments as if statements on the stack name for anything bigger than sizes and counts.
Commit Pulumi.yaml and the Pulumi.<stack>.yaml files of long-lived stacks (secrets in them are encrypted). Ephemeral stacks usually do not commit theirs.
In CI, always pass --stack with the fully qualified name, and run preview in pull requests and up on merge.
Tag stacks (pulumi stack tag set environment production) so Pulumi Cloud can group them. Avoid the reserved prefixes pulumi:, gitHub: and vcs:.
On DIY backends: version the bucket, restrict who can write, and back it up. That bucket is your inventory.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Practice

Sketch the project and stack layout for a system with a shared network, a database, and three services, across dev and production. How many stacks, and which references?
Write the StackReference line a services program needs to read vpcId from the matching infra stack, and justify require_output over get_output.
List what you must do yourself if you choose an S3 DIY backend instead of Pulumi Cloud.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Recall card

Project = directory with Pulumi.yaml (name, runtime). Stack = one configured instance with its own state.
org/project/stack is the full name. DIY backends use the literal organization.
pulumi.export publishes; StackReference.require_output consumes.
Backend = Pulumi Cloud or DIY. refresh syncs state from reality, explicitly. stack migrate moves between backends.

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Configuration and Secrets
A stack differs from its siblings in exactly two places: its state and its configuration. Configuration is how one program becomes a t3.micro in dev and a m7i.large in production without a single if. Some of that configuration is a password, and Pulumi’s secrets system makes sure the password is encrypted in every place it travels to, not just the file you typed it into.

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Learning goals

Set, read and structure stack configuration, and explain key namespaces
Choose between get, require and the *_secret variants, and between stack-level and project-level config
Explain how secret-ness propagates through outputs, and where it does not (resource IDs, apply callbacks)
Pick and change a secrets provider, including for DIY backends

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Configuration: per-stack key/value pairs
Values live in Pulumi.<stack>.yaml next to Pulumi.yaml, and you commit that file. The values drive the program, so they belong in version control alongside it.
pulumi config set aws:region us-west-2      # provider namespace
pulumi config set instanceCount 3           # project namespace (implicit)
pulumi config get instanceCount
pulumi config                               # list; --json for machines
cat id_ed25519.pub | pulumi config set publicKey   # stdin: no shell escaping
config set overwrites an existing value without warning. Review the diff of Pulumi.<stack>.yaml before committing.

Keys and namespaces
Keys are [namespace:]name. With no colon, the namespace is the project name. That is how aws:region and your own region coexist. In the stack file the result looks like:
config:
  aws:region: us-west-2
  webserver:instanceCount: "3"
In code, pulumi.Config() reads the project namespace and pulumi.Config("aws") reads another one. Reusable components should read their own namespace (pulumi.Config("mylib")) so they never collide with the consuming project.


Reading from code
import pulumi

config = pulumi.Config()
name = config.require("name")              # missing -> deployment stops with an explanatory error
count = config.get_int("instanceCount") or 1   # missing -> None, so default it
db_password = config.require_secret("dbPassword")  # Output, marked secret

aws_region = pulumi.Config("aws").require("region")
Use require for anything without a sensible default. A typo in a key should fail the preview, not quietly create one instance in production. Configuration is read-only at run time. Writing config from code is the job of the Automation API.
Environment variables also reach the program (os.environ), but configuration is per-stack, versioned and visible to collaborators, so prefer it.


Structured values
--path treats the key as a path into an object:
pulumi config set --path 'data.active' true
pulumi config set --path 'data.nums[0]' 1
pulumi config set --path 'data.nums[1]' 2
config:
  proj:data:
    active: true      # booleans stay booleans
    nums: [1, 2]      # integer-like values become integers
data = pulumi.Config().require_object("data")
active = data["active"]          # a plain dict, not a Config
require_object returns a plain dictionary. Index into it. You cannot call require on a nested value.


Project-level defaults
Values every stack shares go in Pulumi.yaml, and any stack can override them:
# Pulumi.yaml
config:
  aws:region: us-east-1
  name: BroomeLLC
  data:
    value:            # structured project-level values need this wrapper
      active: true
# Pulumi.dev.yaml: overrides for one stack
config:
  aws:region: us-east-2
  myproject:name: MopLLC
Watch the two syntaxes. The stack file uses project:key with structures nested directly. The project file uses bare key and wraps structures in value:. Project-level config is edited by hand (config set doesn’t write it) and holds plaintext only.
The project file can also type-check stack values:
config:
  name:
    type: string
    description: Base name for resources.
    default: BroomeLLC
  subnets:
    type: array
    items:
      type: string
A stack that sets name to a number then fails at pulumi preview. Type specifications don’t yet cover structured config.


Provider configuration
A provider takes settings from three places: pulumi config set aws:region ..., its environment variables, or constructor arguments. Only the default provider reads stack config. An explicit aws.Provider(...) you create reads nothing from config, so pass its arguments explicitly. To forbid implicit default providers altogether:
config:
  pulumi:disable-default-providers: ["aws", "kubernetes"]   # or ["*"]
pulumi:tags in config applies stack tags on every up or refresh. Removing a key from config does not delete the tag from the stack.

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Secrets

Setting
pulumi config set --secret dbPassword 'S3cr37'
The stack file now holds ciphertext:
config:
  myproject:dbPassword:
    secure: AAABAIIlW0ewSuZ1FJxw/+Rpw6BNqTUvGJ30O8WkpL2hB4aPyS7UU68=
Quote values containing $, ! or #, or pipe them from a file, so the shell doesn’t change them first. Secrets work inside structured config too: pulumi config set --path --secret 'endpoints[0].token' ....
The inverse: the CLI tries to detect values that look like tokens and stops you. When it guesses wrong, use --plaintext.
As documented (not run here), listings and accidental prints are masked:
$ pulumi config
KEY                        VALUE
aws:region                 us-west-1
dbPassword                 [secret]


Secrets are outputs that remember
A secret is an Output with a flag. Pulumi encrypts it wherever it is persisted, and propagates the flag. Anything computed from a secret with apply or Output.all is also secret. Resource properties built from it are encrypted in state.
import pulumi
import pulumi_aws as aws

cfg = pulumi.Config()
param = aws.ssm.Parameter(
    "a-secret-param",
    type="SecureString",
    value=cfg.require_secret("my-secret-value"),   # encrypted in state too
)
Ways to make a value secret:







Source
How




Config
get_secret / require_secret


An existing value
pulumi.Output.secret(value)


A resource’s outputs
ResourceOptions(additional_secret_outputs=["result"])


Derived values
Automatic via apply / Output.all on a secret



Reading a --secret key with plain require hands you the plaintext and drops the marking downstream. Always use the secret getters.


Where secret-ness ends

Inside apply. The callback receives plaintext. Pulumi marks the return value secret, but cannot stop the callback from printing or writing it to a file.
Resource IDs. A resource’s id is always stored in plaintext, and additional_secret_outputs=["id"] does nothing. random.RandomString exposes its result as its ID too, so its value lands unencrypted in state. Use random.RandomPassword and mark result secret.
Outside the stack. Secret-ness covers one stack’s state. Sharing the same credential across stacks or teams is a job for Pulumi ESC environments, which a stack imports with an environment: list in its stack file. Explicit stack config wins over imported values.



Secrets providers
By default with Pulumi Cloud, each stack gets its own Cloud-managed key and each value a nonce. Choose another provider when you use a DIY backend or your organisation mandates its own KMS:
pulumi stack init prod --secrets-provider="awskms://alias/pulumi-prod?region=us-east-1"
pulumi stack init prod --secrets-provider="gcpkms://projects/P/locations/L/keyRings/R/cryptoKeys/K"
pulumi stack init prod --secrets-provider="azurekeyvault://myvault.vault.azure.net/keys/pulumi"
pulumi stack init prod --secrets-provider="hashivault://pulumi-prod"
pulumi stack init prod --secrets-provider=passphrase

awskms accepts an ID, alias or ARN, an optional profile=, and (CLI v3.41.1+) context_<k>=<v> encryption context you can condition IAM policies on.
hashivault reads VAULT_SERVER_URL and VAULT_SERVER_TOKEN.
passphrase derives the key from a passphrase you supply (typically through PULUMI_CONFIG_PASSPHRASE). Lose it and the stack’s secrets are unrecoverable.

The provider’s public bits (encryptionsalt for passphrase, encryptedkey for KMS-style providers) are written into Pulumi.<stack>.yaml and are safe to commit. To switch an existing stack:
pulumi stack change-secrets-provider "awskms://alias/pulumi-prod?region=us-east-1"
pulumi preview      # expect: no changes
This re-encrypts config and state. If you’d rather not commit stack files at all, pulumi config refresh rebuilds them from the last deployment.

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Diagnosis








Symptom
Likely cause
Fix




“Missing required configuration variable”
Key not set for this stack, or wrong namespace
pulumi config -s <stack>; check the project: prefix


Value set, program says unset
Set under a different stack, or project renamed
Confirm the active stack; rename keys in the stack file


Password visible in stack export
Read with require instead of require_secret, or carried in an id
Use the secret getters; avoid ID-bearing resources


CLI refuses a harmless value as “looks like a secret”
Secret detection heuristic
--plaintext


“passphrase must be set” or decrypt fails in CI
Passphrase or KMS access missing in the runner
Provide PULUMI_CONFIG_PASSPHRASE or KMS credentials


Preview fails with a type error
Project-level type spec
Fix the stack value’s type

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Operational care

Commit Pulumi.yaml and Pulumi.<stack>.yaml. Ciphertext is meant to be committed. Never commit plaintext you meant to mark secret, because git history keeps it.
Treat pulumi config set in pipelines as a code change. Prefer reviewing the stack file in a PR to mutating config during deploys.
Use one KMS key or ESC environment per trust boundary (prod versus non-prod), and restrict decrypt rights accordingly.
Rotate by setting the new value with --secret and running up. Changing the provider is a separate operation (change-secrets-provider).

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Practice

Design config for a service with region, instance count, a list of allowed CIDRs, and a database password. Which keys go project-level, which stack-level, and which are secret?
A colleague creates a token with random.RandomString and marks result secret. What is still exposed, and what do you change?
Your team moves from Pulumi Cloud to an S3 DIY backend. What happens to secrets, and which provider would you pick?

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Recall card

Pulumi.<stack>.yaml holds per-stack config (commit it). Pulumi.yaml config: holds shared, plaintext, typed defaults.
No-colon keys belong to the project. Config("ns") reads other namespaces.
require fails loudly, get returns None, and *_secret keeps the marking.
Secret-ness propagates through outputs, except inside apply callbacks and resource IDs.
Use --secrets-provider at stack init and stack change-secrets-provider later. A passphrase is a key you must not lose.

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
A Pulumi program looks imperative: Python statements, run top to bottom. The infrastructure it describes is declarative: Pulumi decides what to create, in what order, and what to leave alone. The bridge between the two is a pair of types. Inputs are what you give a resource. Outputs are values the cloud reports back later. Every confusing moment for new Pulumi users (“why does my bucket name print as an object?”) comes from treating an output as if it were already a value.

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Learning goals

Distinguish inputs, resource outputs and stack outputs
Explain how passing an output into an input creates a dependency edge
Transform outputs with apply, Output.all, Output.format, Output.concat and the JSON helpers, and reach nested values by lifting
Recognise the “output used as a plain value” bug, and why resources must not be created inside apply

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Inputs
An input is an argument to a resource, usually one parameter of the underlying cloud API call. Every input of type Input[T] also accepts a plain T:
import pulumi_random as random

my_id = random.RandomId("mine", byte_length=8)   # 8 is a plain value used as an input
Python offers two spellings for object-shaped inputs: an ...Args class or a dictionary typed as ...ArgsDict. Both carry the same fields, and the dictionary form is shorter:
import pulumi_aws as aws

repo = aws.ecr.Repository(
    "repo",
    image_tag_mutability="MUTABLE",
    image_scanning_configuration={"scan_on_push": True},
)

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Outputs
An output is a property the provider reports after the resource exists, such as an ID, an ARN, an endpoint or a generated password. Outputs behave like futures. During a first pulumi up the value is unknown until the cloud answers. During pulumi preview it may never be known.
Pass an output straight into another resource’s input and Pulumi records a dependency:
import pulumi_aws as aws
import pulumi_random as random

password = random.RandomPassword("password", length=16, special=True)

db = aws.rds.Instance(
    "db",
    instance_class="db.t3.micro",
    allocated_storage=64,
    engine="mysql",
    username="someone",
    password=password.result,      # output -> input: an edge in the graph
)
That edge tells Pulumi to create the password before the database, and on destroy to delete the database before the password. You wrote no ordering code. A program that wires outputs to inputs gets correct ordering for free, and depends_on is only for dependencies that no value carries.
Three similar names refer to different things:







Term
What it is




Input
An argument to a resource; accepts plain values or outputs


Resource output
A property of a resource, known once the provider reports it


Stack output
A value you pulumi.export at the end of a run for the CLI or a StackReference

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Getting at the value
Because an output is not yet a value, you can’t use ordinary language operations on it. print(bucket.id) or "https://" + lb.dns_name doesn’t do what you expect. The SDK supplies the tools instead.

apply: transform one output
url = lb.dns_name.apply(lambda name: f"https://{name}")
The callback runs when the value is known and receives the plain value. Its return value becomes a new Output, which you can pass on as an input or export. Secret-ness and dependencies flow through.


Output.all: combine several
import pulumi

conn = pulumi.Output.all(server.name, database.name).apply(
    lambda args: f"Server=tcp:{args[0]}.database.windows.net;initial catalog={args[1]};"
)

# keyword form yields a dict
conn = pulumi.Output.all(server=server.name, db=database.name).apply(
    lambda a: f"Server=tcp:{a['server']}.database.windows.net;initial catalog={a['db']};"
)


Helpers: skip the lambda
Most apply calls build a string or some JSON. The helpers do that directly and are easier to read:
import json
import pulumi

url = pulumi.Output.format("https://{0}/api", lb.dns_name)
arn_path = pulumi.Output.concat(bucket.arn, "/*")

policy = pulumi.Output.json_dumps({
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [{
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Principal": "*",
        "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
        "Resource": [arn_path],          # outputs allowed inside the structure
    }],
})

parsed = pulumi.Output.json_loads(some_json_output)
json_dumps accepts a structure that has outputs nested inside it. A json.dumps inside an apply would make you resolve each one by hand first.


Lifting: reach into nested outputs
Properties and indexes can be read straight off an output, with no apply. Pulumi “lifts” the access:
record_name = cert.domain_validation_options[0].resource_record_name
Without lifting this would be cert.domain_validation_options.apply(lambda o: o[0].resource_record_name).

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
section: Two rules that prevent most bugs
text:
Two rules that prevent most bugs
1. Never treat an output as a plain value. Printing it, concatenating it with +, using it in an if, or formatting it with an f-string outside apply gives you the wrapper object, not the value. Python’s Output warns when converted to a string, and the result ends up in resource names and tags looking like garbage. Use apply, format, concat or json_dumps.
2. Don’t create resources inside apply or all. Pulumi’s documentation says to avoid it wherever possible. Resources created in a callback don’t appear in pulumi preview unless the value is already known, so the preview stops matching what up will do. Reviewers then approve a plan that leaves things out. If the number of resources depends on a value, read that value from configuration (known at preview), not from another resource’s output.

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Resource identity
Wiring resources means passing some identifier, and the inputs differ in which one they want. A resource has four identities: its logical name (the first constructor argument), its physical name at the provider, its physical ID (resource.id), and its Pulumi URN. Many inputs want an ARN, an endpoint or a name instead of the ID. A type mismatch at preview usually means you passed the wrong identity. Check the input’s documentation.

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Diagnosis








Symptom
Cause
Fix




A name or tag contains text about calling __str__ on an Output
Output used in an f-string or str()
Output.format/concat, or build it in apply


Preview shows fewer resources than up creates
Resources created inside apply
Drive counts from config. Create resources at top level


Resources created in the wrong order
The dependency is not carried by any value
Pass the output as an input, or depends_on as a last resort


Type error passing bucket where a string is expected
Passed the resource, not a property
bucket.id, bucket.arn or bucket.bucket, per the input’s docs


JSON policy has a placeholder where an ARN belongs
json.dumps on a structure containing outputs
Output.json_dumps

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Practice

Build an output URL https://<dns>/health from a load balancer’s dns_name three ways: apply, Output.format and Output.concat. Which reads best?
A colleague loops for i in range(int(count_output)). Explain why this fails and rewrite it to use config.
Write an S3 bucket policy that references two buckets’ ARNs, using only Output.json_dumps.

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Recall card

Inputs accept plain values or outputs. Outputs are future values reported by the provider.
Output to input means a dependency edge. Ordering for create and destroy is automatic.
apply handles one output, Output.all several, and format/concat/json_dumps/json_loads are the common shortcuts. Lifting reads nested fields.
Never treat an output as plain, and never create resources inside apply.

title: Unit Testing Pulumi Programs with Mocks
text:
Unit Testing Pulumi Programs with Mocks
After reading this chapter, you will be able to write fast, isolated unit tests for Pulumi infrastructure programs using Pulumi’s built-in Python mock engine and standard test frameworks such as unittest and pytest. You will learn how to intercept cloud resource allocations and API invokes, validate configuration invariants and tagging policies, catch security misconfigurations before running a cloud preview, and handle Python asynchronous test execution correctly.

title: Unit Testing Pulumi Programs with Mocks
text:
Why test with mocks?
Deploying infrastructure to a cloud sandbox to verify logic takes minutes per test run, requires active AWS credentials, and incurs cloud billing. Even a local dry run like pulumi preview requires an authenticated session, network access to cloud APIs, and a state backend.
Unit testing with mocks solves a different problem: verifying that your program generates the intended resource definitions, flags, and relationships before contacting a provider. Pulumi executes your program in an in-memory test harness where:

Cloud API calls are intercepted without making network connections.
Mock handlers return synthesized IDs and attributes.
Tests execute in milliseconds within standard CI pipelines.
Security and compliance regressions are caught directly on developer machines.

Testing with mocks does not validate that AWS will accept an argument or that an IAM policy grants sufficient runtime privileges; that remains the domain of integration tests. Mocks validate the logic of your program.

title: Unit Testing Pulumi Programs with Mocks
text:
The Pulumi mock runtime
The Pulumi Python SDK provides the pulumi.runtime.Mocks base class. When a Pulumi program instantiates resources or invokes provider functions, the SDK passes those requests to a registered subclass of Mocks.
A complete mock implementation overrides two methods:
class pulumi.runtime.Mocks:
    def new_resource(self, args: pulumi.runtime.MockResourceArgs) -> list:
        ...

    def call(self, args: pulumi.runtime.MockCallArgs) -> dict:
        ...









Method
Intercepts
Argument fields
Expected return value




new_resource
Resource declarations (aws.s3.Bucket, aws.ec2.Instance, etc.)
args.typ: resource type token (e.g. aws:ec2/instance:Instance)args.name: logical name in Pulumi programargs.inputs: dictionary of input propertiesargs.provider: provider referenceargs.id_: existing resource ID if any
A two-element list: [resource_id, state_dict]


call
Function invokes (aws.ec2.get_ami, aws.get_caller_identity, etc.)
args.token: function token (e.g. aws:ec2/getAmi:getAmi)args.args: dictionary of call argumentsargs.provider: provider reference
A dictionary containing output attributes of the invoke



Once you define a mock class, you register it with pulumi.runtime.set_mocks(MyMocks(), preview=False).

Registering mocks before program execution
The call to pulumi.runtime.set_mocks() must happen before your infrastructure module executes. If a resource or function runs before mocks are registered, the SDK attempts to connect to a live Pulumi engine RPC server and immediately fails.
Because Pulumi resources instantiate upon module import, you should not import your infrastructure module (__main__ or your stack file) at the top of your test file. Instead, configure mocks inside the test setup phase and evaluate the program dynamically using runpy.run_path().

title: Unit Testing Pulumi Programs with Mocks
text:
Async testing with IsolatedAsyncioTestCase
Every Pulumi resource property is an Output[T], which behaves like an asynchronous promise. To assert against values inside an Output, your test must inspect the output through .apply().
The recommended pattern in modern Python combines unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase with the @pulumi.runtime.test decorator:

Subclass unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase.
In setUp(), invoke pulumi.runtime.set_mocks(MyMocks(), preview=False).
Load the infrastructure program using runpy.run_path("__main__.py").
Decorate each test method with @pulumi.runtime.test.
Return the resolved Output from the test method so the runner awaits its assertions.


Python 3.14 event loop requirements
On Python 3.14 and later, calling asyncio.get_event_loop() without an active event loop in the main thread raises RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread 'MainThread'. If pulumi.runtime.set_mocks() is called at module level outside of an active event loop, the test runner fails immediately.
Using unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase manages the event loop lifecycle automatically for each test method. If you use a plain function-based test harness, you must call asyncio.set_event_loop(asyncio.new_event_loop()) before calling set_mocks().

title: Unit Testing Pulumi Programs with Mocks
section: Lab: testing an AWS infrastructure stack

title: Unit Testing Pulumi Programs with Mocks
text:
Fixing the infrastructure flaw
To resolve the violation, we restrict port 22 access to the internal corporate CIDR 10.0.0.0/8. Here is the complete corrected program.

import pulumi
import pulumi_aws as aws

ami = aws.ec2.get_ami(
    most_recent=True,
    owners=["amazon"],
    filters=[
        aws.ec2.GetAmiFilterArgs(
            name="name",
            values=["al2023-ami-*-x86_64"],
        )
    ],
)

web_sg = aws.ec2.SecurityGroup(
    "web-sg",
    description="Allow HTTP and SSH access",
    ingress=[
        aws.ec2.SecurityGroupIngressArgs(
            protocol="tcp",
            from_port=80,
            to_port=80,
            cidr_blocks=["0.0.0.0/0"],
        ),
        aws.ec2.SecurityGroupIngressArgs(
            protocol="tcp",
            from_port=22,
            to_port=22,
            cidr_blocks=["10.0.0.0/8"],  # Fixed: restricted to internal CIDR
        ),
    ],
)

instance = aws.ec2.Instance(
    "web",
    instance_type="t3.micro",
    ami=ami.id,
    vpc_security_group_ids=[web_sg.id],
    tags={
        "Name": "web",
        "team": "platform",
    },
)

bucket = aws.s3.Bucket(
    "logs",
    tags={
        "team": "platform",
    },
)

pulumi.export("instance_id", instance.id)
pulumi.export("bucket_arn", bucket.arn)
Run the tests inside the fixed directory by reusing test_infra.py:
cd fixed && cp ../test_infra.py . && python -m pytest -q -p no:warnings --tb=line test_infra.py
The command produced the following output:
....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed in 0.95s
All four unit tests now execute and pass without contacting AWS or requiring the Pulumi CLI.

title: Unit Testing Pulumi Programs with Mocks
text:
How mock outputs resolve
When writing assertions inside check callbacks, remember how Pulumi outputs behave in tests:

Synthetic State: When new_resource returns [id, state], the SDK populates the created resource’s properties with the keys provided in state. If your mock does not include an expected output field (for example, public_ip), accessing that attribute yields None or an unknown output.
Preview Mode: The parameter preview=False in pulumi.runtime.set_mocks(MyMocks(), preview=False) treats all mocked resource inputs as known. If set to True, computed values behave as unknowns, mirroring pulumi preview. For unit testing configuration policies, preview=False is standard.
Property Normalization: Input property names in Pulumi resources often use Python snake_case (such as cidr_blocks), but provider states may store camelCase keys (cidrBlocks). Checking both forms in your assertions ensures resilient tests across SDK schema versions.

title: Unit Testing Pulumi Programs with Mocks
text:
Pitfalls








Mistake
Manifestation
Remedy




Importing __main__ at module top-level
Tests crash with RPC connection errors to the Pulumi engine daemon
Register mocks in setUp() and load the program dynamically using runpy.run_path()


Calling set_mocks at module level on Python 3.14+
RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread 'MainThread'
Use unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase so each test runs inside an established event loop


Forgetting to return the output promise from @pulumi.runtime.test
Tests exit prematurely without evaluating assertions in .apply()
Always return resource.property.apply(check) from the decorated test method


Asserting on resource outputs not defined in new_resource
Attribute resolves to None or an empty value
Include expected output attributes (e.g. arn, id) in the dictionary returned by new_resource


Attempting to validate provider behavior with unit mocks
Test passes, but cloud deployment fails due to invalid parameters
Use unit mocks to verify program declarations; use integration tests for provider compliance

title: Unit Testing Pulumi Programs with Mocks
text:
Summary

Pulumi unit tests intercept resource definitions and function calls entirely in memory, requiring neither the Pulumi CLI nor cloud provider credentials.
The pulumi.runtime.Mocks class provides new_resource to simulate resource states and call to simulate provider lookup functions.
Mocks must be configured using pulumi.runtime.set_mocks() before executing infrastructure definitions.
unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase provides clean event loop isolation on modern Python versions (including Python 3.14).
Tests inspect resource state by passing assertions into Output.apply() inside methods decorated with @pulumi.runtime.test.

title: Component Resources
text:
Component Resources
After this page you can group related resources into a typed Python component resource, parent its children correctly, know which resource options reach those children, expose a secret output, validate arguments before anything is registered, unit-test the component with Pulumi’s mocks, and rename it later without replacing what it manages.

title: Component Resources
text:
Thesis
As infrastructure programs expand, instantiating low-level cloud primitives repeatedly leads to duplication, inconsistent security defaults, and brittle code. A plain Python function that returns resources lets you reuse code, but Pulumi itself never sees the grouping: the resources land flat in the stack, with nothing in the state or the CLI that ties them together.
Component resources solve this by inheriting from pulumi.ComponentResource. They introduce a custom type token into the resource graph, group child resources under a single parent identity, and give you one object to pass options to and to unit-test.

title: Component Resources
text:
Why components? (vs functions returning resources)
When structuring reusable infrastructure constructs, developers often start by wrapping resource definitions inside standard Python functions. While simple, helper functions have structural limitations compared to ComponentResource classes.
# Helper function approach
def create_service_credentials(name: str, service: str):
    user = random.RandomPet(f"{name}-user", length=2)
    pwd = random.RandomPassword(f"{name}-password", length=24)
    return user, pwd
Comparing the two approaches across key architectural dimensions highlights why custom component resources are preferred for reusable infrastructure patterns:








Aspect
Helper function
Component resource




State
Each resource sits directly under the stack
One parent entry with the children nested under it


CLI tree view
A flat list
A subtree under the component


Options
Pass opts to every resource yourself
Several options set on the component (such as providers and protect) are inherited by its children


Type identity
None; you get back a tuple
Its own type token, such as acme:index:ServiceCredentials


Child-wide changes
Edit every call site
transforms on the component can rewrite each child as it registers



Helper functions leave child resources floating at the root level of the Pulumi stack graph. A component gives them an owner, so previews and diffs read in the same units you think in.

title: Component Resources
text:
The type token
Every Pulumi resource has a type token of the form package:module:type. Pulumi’s own component guide uses index as the module for a component defined at the top level of a package, and this page follows that convention:
<package>:index:<ComponentName>
So in acme:index:ServiceCredentials, acme is your package or organisation namespace, index is the module, and ServiceCredentials is the type name.
The type token is part of the component’s URN. Every child’s URN contains it too, as you will see in the test output below. Change the token after deploying and Pulumi sees a new component with new children: it plans to create those and delete the old ones, unless you add an alias (covered later on this page).

title: Component Resources
text:
The component
The following module defines ServiceCredentials, a component resource grouping a random pet name and password generation for a target service.

"""A component resource that groups the random resources one service needs."""
import pulumi
import pulumi_random as random


class ServiceCredentialsArgs:
    def __init__(self, service: str, password_length: int = 24):
        if password_length < 16:
            raise ValueError("password_length must be at least 16")
        self.service = service
        self.password_length = password_length


class ServiceCredentials(pulumi.ComponentResource):
    username: pulumi.Output[str]
    password: pulumi.Output[str]

    def __init__(self, name: str, args: ServiceCredentialsArgs,
                 opts: pulumi.ResourceOptions | None = None):
        super().__init__("acme:index:ServiceCredentials", name, None, opts)

        child = pulumi.ResourceOptions(parent=self)

        suffix = random.RandomPet(f"{name}-user", length=2, separator="-",
                                  opts=child)
        password = random.RandomPassword(f"{name}-password",
                                         length=args.password_length,
                                         special=False, opts=child)

        self.pet = suffix
        self.username = suffix.id.apply(lambda pet: f"{args.service}-{pet}")
        self.password = pulumi.Output.secret(password.result)

        self.register_outputs({
            "username": self.username,
            "password": self.password,
        })

Code Walk-Through

Argument Class (ServiceCredentialsArgs): Holds the component’s inputs and validates them before any resource exists. A password_length below 16 raises ValueError right away.
Component Inheritance (pulumi.ComponentResource): The component extends ComponentResource and sets its outputs as class-level type annotations (pulumi.Output[str]).
super().__init__ Call: Initializes the underlying Pulumi resource engine with the type token "acme:index:ServiceCredentials", the logical resource name, no input properties (None), and optional pulumi.ResourceOptions.
Parenting Child Resources: child = pulumi.ResourceOptions(parent=self) creates a shared options instance. Passing opts=child to random.RandomPet and random.RandomPassword nests them under this component instance.
Dynamic Naming: Child resource logical names are dynamically formatted using f"{name}-user" and f"{name}-password". With hard-coded child names, a second instance in the same stack would try to register duplicate URNs.
Secret Output Wrappers: pulumi.Output.secret(password.result) marks the generated output as sensitive, so Pulumi encrypts it in the state and masks it in CLI output.
self.register_outputs(...): Tells Pulumi the component has finished registering its children and records its outputs.

title: Component Resources
section: register_outputs and what breaks without it
text:
register_outputs and what breaks without it
Pulumi’s component guide puts it this way: calling register_outputs at the end of the constructor “signals Pulumi that the process of creating the component resource has completed”. The dictionary you pass is stored as the component’s outputs in the stack state. The child resources have their own state and are not affected.
Call it at the end of every component constructor, even with an empty dictionary. Leave it out and Pulumi has no explicit signal that the component is finished, and the component’s outputs are never recorded.

title: Component Resources
section: Options that do and do not apply
text:
Options that do and do not apply
A component has no cloud provider behind it, so options that change provider behaviour have no direct effect on the component itself. Pulumi’s resource options reference lists which options a component passes on to its children:







Option set on the component
Inherited by its children?




providers, provider
Yes (but provider has no effect on the component itself; Pulumi recommends providers for components)


protect, retain_on_delete
Yes


aliases, deleted_with
Yes


transforms
Yes


depends_on
No


ignore_changes, custom_timeouts, replace_on_changes, hooks
No



For an option that is not inherited, set it on the children yourself, or use a transform on the component to add it to each child as that child registers:
# Add ignore_changes to every RandomPassword created under the component
def ignore_password_length(args: pulumi.ResourceTransformArgs):
    if args.type_ == "random:index/randomPassword:RandomPassword":
        return pulumi.ResourceTransformResult(
            props=args.props,
            opts=pulumi.ResourceOptions.merge(
                args.opts, pulumi.ResourceOptions(ignore_changes=["length"])),
        )
    return None

creds = ServiceCredentials(
    "api", ServiceCredentialsArgs(service="billing"),
    opts=pulumi.ResourceOptions(transforms=[ignore_password_length]))
This snippet follows the transforms documentation and was not run here.

title: Component Resources
text:
Visualizing the resource tree






Note



Not run here. The Pulumi CLI is not installed on the machine used for this page, so no pulumi preview or pulumi up was run. The tree below shows the shape of that output (an illustration, not a captured run). The URN further down is real; it comes from the unit tests later on this page.


pulumi up draws the component as a parent with its children indented beneath it:
Type                                 Name            Status
pulumi:pulumi:Stack                  my-project-dev
└─ acme:index:ServiceCredentials     api             created
   ├─ random:index:RandomPet         api-user        created
   └─ random:index:RandomPassword    api-password    created
A child’s URN records the hierarchy by putting its parent’s type token in front of its own type, joined with $:
urn:pulumi:stack::project::acme:index:ServiceCredentials$random:index/randomPet:RandomPet::api-user

title: Component Resources
text:
Testing component resources
Unit testing component resources requires mocking the Pulumi runtime engine calls.

Complete Test Suite
The following listing tests the ServiceCredentials component without calling any real cloud endpoints.

import asyncio

import pulumi

# Python 3.14 no longer creates an event loop on demand; Pulumi's mocks need one.
asyncio.set_event_loop(asyncio.new_event_loop())


class Mocks(pulumi.runtime.Mocks):
    calls = []

    def new_resource(self, args: pulumi.runtime.MockResourceArgs):
        Mocks.calls.append((args.typ, args.name, args.custom))
        outputs = dict(args.inputs)
        if args.typ == "random:index/randomPet:RandomPet":
            return [f"{args.name}_id", outputs]
        if args.typ == "random:index/randomPassword:RandomPassword":
            outputs["result"] = "x" * int(args.inputs["length"])
        return [f"{args.name}_id", outputs]

    def call(self, args: pulumi.runtime.MockCallArgs):
        return {}


pulumi.runtime.set_mocks(Mocks(), preview=False)

import pytest  # noqa: E402
from credentials import ServiceCredentials, ServiceCredentialsArgs  # noqa: E402


@pulumi.runtime.test
def test_children_are_parented_to_the_component():
    creds = ServiceCredentials("api", ServiceCredentialsArgs(service="billing"))

    def check(args):
        urn, pet_urn, username = args
        print("component URN:", urn)
        print("child URN:    ", pet_urn)
        print("username:     ", username)
        for typ, name, custom in Mocks.calls:
            print(f"registered {typ} name={name} custom={custom}")
        assert urn.endswith("acme:index:ServiceCredentials::api")
        assert pet_urn.endswith("::acme:index:ServiceCredentials$random:index/randomPet:RandomPet::api-user")
        assert username == "billing-api-user_id"

    return pulumi.Output.all(creds.urn, creds.pet.urn, creds.username).apply(check)


@pulumi.runtime.test
def test_password_is_secret_and_long_enough():
    creds = ServiceCredentials("db", ServiceCredentialsArgs(service="orders",
                                                            password_length=32))

    def check(args):
        password, is_secret = args
        assert len(password) == 32
        assert is_secret

    return pulumi.Output.all(creds.password,
                             pulumi.Output.from_input(
                                 creds.password).is_secret()).apply(check)


def test_short_passwords_are_rejected():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="at least 16"):
        ServiceCredentialsArgs(service="x", password_length=8)


Two Critical Testing Pitfalls

1. Python 3.14 Event Loop Initialization
Since Python 3.14, asyncio.get_event_loop() raises RuntimeError when there is no current event loop, instead of creating one. Pulumi’s mock setup asks for the current loop, so on Python 3.14 the tests fail before they start unless one has been set. Here is python -m pytest -q -s test_credentials.py with the set_event_loop line removed:
    raise RuntimeError('There is no current event loop in thread %r.'
E   RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread 'MainThread'.
ERROR test_credentials.py - RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in t...
1 error in 0.18s
To resolve this, explicitly instantiate and set an event loop before invoking set_mocks:
asyncio.set_event_loop(asyncio.new_event_loop())


2. Race Conditions in Mock Assertions
In the first version of the test, the apply hung off creds.urn alone. It ran as soon as the component’s URN resolved, before the children had registered, so Mocks.calls held only the component. Wait on child outputs as well before you inspect what was registered:
return pulumi.Output.all(creds.urn, creds.pet.urn, creds.username).apply(check)



Running the Tests
The versions used (python -c "import sys, pulumi, pytest; print(sys.version.split()[0], pulumi.__version__, pytest.__version__)"):
Python 3.14.8
pulumi                                   3.273.0
pulumi-random                            4.21.6
pytest                                   9.2.0
Run the suite with python -m pytest -q -s test_credentials.py:
component URN: urn:pulumi:stack::project::pulumi:pulumi:Stack$acme:index:ServiceCredentials::api
child URN:     urn:pulumi:stack::project::acme:index:ServiceCredentials$random:index/randomPet:RandomPet::api-user
username:      billing-api-user_id
registered acme:index:ServiceCredentials name=api custom=False
registered random:index/randomPet:RandomPet name=api-user custom=True
...
3 passed in 0.11s
exit status: 0
In the output, Mocks.new_resource sees both kinds of resource: - The component resource (custom=False, type acme:index:ServiceCredentials). - The child resources (custom=True, types random:index/randomPet:RandomPet and random:index/randomPassword:RandomPassword).

title: Component Resources
text:
Evolving a component resource
Components get renamed and reorganised. Each of those changes alters URNs, and a changed URN looks to Pulumi like a delete and a create unless you tell it otherwise.

Using Aliases for Component Renames
If a component’s name or type token changes, give the old identity as an alias:
# Alias old component type token to prevent recreation during updates
alias_option = pulumi.Alias(type_="acme:index:OldServiceCredentials")
super().__init__(
    "acme:index:ServiceCredentials",
    name,
    None,
    opts=pulumi.ResourceOptions.merge(opts, pulumi.ResourceOptions(aliases=[alias_option]))
)


State Migrations for Child Restructuring
When a child moves to a different parent, alias its old parent. pulumi.Alias(parent=...) accepts either a resource or a URN string:
child_alias = pulumi.Alias(parent=old_parent_urn)  # URN string of the old parent
suffix = random.RandomPet(
    f"{name}-user",
    length=2,
    opts=pulumi.ResourceOptions(parent=self, aliases=[child_alias])
)
An alias tells Pulumi that the new URN is the same resource it already tracks, so it updates the state instead of replacing the resource. Aliases set on a component are inherited by its children, so a component rename carries the children with it. Run pulumi preview and check for zero replacements before you up. (Aliases were not exercised here; there is no CLI on this machine.)

title: Component Resources
text:
Common mistakes








Anti-Pattern / Error
Consequence
Correct Pattern




Omitting parent=self on child resources
Children sit at the stack root and inherit nothing from the component
Pass opts=pulumi.ResourceOptions(parent=self) to every child


Hard-coding child logical names
Duplicate URN errors when instantiating multiple instances of the component
Prefix child names with the component instance name (f"{name}-child")


Forgetting self.register_outputs({...})
Pulumi gets no explicit signal that the component is done, and its outputs are not recorded
Call self.register_outputs(...) at the end of the constructor


Passing provider= to a component
No effect on the component itself
Use providers=[my_provider] (or a map) on components


Changing type token without an Alias
Pulumi recreates component and all nested child resources
Pass old type tokens in aliases=[Alias(type_="...")]


Asserting Mocks.calls without waiting on children
Test runs before child resources register in mock list
Include child outputs in Output.all(...) before asserting calls

title: Component Resources
text:
Practice

Modify credentials.py to add an optional prefix string argument to ServiceCredentialsArgs. If supplied, prepend the prefix to username. Add a unit test in test_credentials.py asserting that prefixes format correctly.
Add a connection_string output built with pulumi.Output.format, check that it stays secret, and include it in register_outputs.
Write a test showing that password_length=16 (the boundary) is accepted and gives a 16-character password under the mocks.

title: Component Resources
text:
Key takeaways

Components subclass pulumi.ComponentResource and group related child infrastructure resources into a typed abstraction.
Use type tokens of the form <package>:index:<Name>. Changing one changes every URN under it, so add an alias when you do.
Child resources must specify parent=self and incorporate name into their logical names to preserve hierarchy and prevent URN collisions.
End every constructor with self.register_outputs(...).
providers, protect, aliases and transforms reach the children; depends_on and ignore_changes do not, so use a transform for those.
Under mocks, new_resource sees the component (custom=False) as well as its children (custom=True). Python 3.14+ test suites must set an asyncio event loop explicitly before calling set_mocks.

title: Component Resources
text:
